newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Greek minister dismisses Turkey's NATO veto threat.
newsitem.headline: Greek minister dismisses Turkey's NATO veto threat.

text.p: Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos said on Monday he considers Turkey's threat to veto NATO expansion to former Communist countries if Ankara does not gain European Union membership as frivolous.
Speaking at a joint news conference with Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec, Pangalos rejected any connection between NATO expansion and Turkey's attempts to join the EU.
"I take everthing that Turkey does and says very seriously, but on this particular point I see that no one takes them seriously," Pangalos said.
"I tend also to see no relationship between NATO and the enlargement of the European Union. That is a separate process."
In January, Turkey threatened to block NATO expansion unless it obtained membership in the EU where Greece -- which has long resisted Ankara's attempts to join the Union -- is a member.

Leaders of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) -- in which both Greece and Turkey are members -- are expected to name a group of former communist countries to join the alliance at a July summit in Madrid.
Poland, Hungary, and the Czechs are seen as top contenders, and Pangalos said on Monday he supported Prague's aim to join both the security alliance and the EU "as soon as possible".
Under NATO consensus rules, any member state can single-handedly block major decisions of the alliance.
The Greek minister said it would be a "very original diplomatic practice" if any state used a veto in one organisation for something it wants in another.
Greece has been fiercely at odds with Turkey since 1974 when Turkish troops invaded Cyprus and have since occupied the northern third of the Mediterranean island.

Greek and Turkish warships nearly clashed last year over a small deserted islet in the Aegean sea which separates the two countries, but war was averted after a last-minute diplomatic intervention by the United States.
While Athens rejects Ankara's bid for EU membership, it backs that of the relatively prosperous Cyprus, whose Greek-led authority is the only internationally recognised government.
